summary.text: Arachnids are arthropods of the class Arachnida, a group that includes spiders, scorpions, ticks, mites and harvestmen.
Almost all adult arachnids have eight legs, unlike adult insects, which have six, and arachnids have no antennae or wings.
Their body has two sections, a cephalothorax and an abdomen, and almost all living arachnids are terrestrial.

facts.label: First appendage pair
facts.value: The chelicerae, used in feeding and defense

facts.label: Scorpion stinger
facts.value: A telson modified into a stinger

items.prompt: You catch a small creature with eight legs, no antennae and no wings. Which describes it best?

options.label: An insect, since adult insects have eight legs
An arachnid, since adults have eight legs and lack antennae and wings
An insect, since all insects lack wings and antennae
A scorpion, since only scorpions have eight legs

items.explain: Almost all adult arachnids have eight legs, while adult insects have six, and arachnids have neither antennae nor wings.

items.prompt: The pinchers at the front of a scorpion are formed by which pair of appendages?

options.label: The pedipalps
The chelicerae
The pectines
The spinnerets

items.explain: In scorpions the pedipalps end in a pair of pinchers. The chelicerae are the first pair and serve in feeding and defense.

items.prompt: A desert arachnid loses very little water through its body. Which adaptation helps it?

options.label: Gills along the sides of its abdomen, which trap moisture
Wings that carry it between far-apart sources of water
A waxy layer over its cuticle and efficient excretory structures
Antennae that detect water from far across the sand

items.explain: Water conservation on land is aided by a waxy layer covering the cuticle and efficient excretory structures.

items.prompt: Most arachnids lack extensor muscles in the outer joints of their legs. How does a spider straighten its legs?

options.label: It tightens the cartilage-like tissue inside its body
It pulls its legs straight with elastic joints, as solifuges do
It relies on muscles that extend two joints at once
It uses the pressure of its body fluid to push the limbs out

items.explain: Spiders and whip scorpions extend their limbs hydraulically using the pressure of their hemolymph.

items.prompt: Under a microscope, a mite larva has only six legs. What would you usually expect after it moults into a nymph?

options.label: It loses its legs entirely
A fourth pair of legs usually appears
It grows a pair of antennae
It stays at six legs for life

items.explain: The larvae of mites have six legs, and a fourth pair usually appears when they moult into nymphs.

items.prompt: Why do some scientists question the name cephalothorax for the front section of an arachnid?

options.label: No fossil or embryo shows that a separate thorax-like division ever existed
The front section has no legs attached to it
The front section is covered by many separate plates
The front section is found only in scorpions

items.explain: The name implies a fused head and thorax, but there is neither fossil nor embryological evidence that arachnids ever had a separate thorax-like division.

paragraphs.heading: What an arachnid is
paragraphs.text: Arachnids are arthropods that make up the class Arachnida, within the subphylum Chelicerata. The class takes in spiders and scorpions, ticks and mites, harvestmen, pseudoscorpions and several less familiar groups. More than 110,000 species have been named, and 51,000 of them are spiders. The name comes from the Greek word for spider, aráchnē, after the myth of Arachne, a proud human weaver who was turned into a spider.

paragraphs.heading: Eight legs and more
paragraphs.text: Almost all adult arachnids have eight legs, while adult insects all have six. Unlike insects, arachnids also have no antennae and no wings. They do carry two extra pairs of appendages. The first pair, the chelicerae, are used in feeding and defense, and the second, the pedipalps, may help with feeding, moving about or reproduction. In the Solifugae the palps look so much like legs that these animals seem to have ten.

paragraphs.heading: Two body sections
paragraphs.text: An arachnid's body has two sections, the prosoma and the opisthosoma, also known as the cephalothorax and the abdomen. Those second names are questioned. Cephalothorax suggests a head joined to a thorax, yet no fossil or embryo evidence shows that arachnids ever had a separate thorax. The front section is usually covered by a single carapace without segments. Apart from the spinnerets of spiders and a pair of pectines on scorpions, the abdomen carries no appendages.

paragraphs.heading: Straightening a leg
paragraphs.text: Like every arthropod, an arachnid has an exoskeleton, and it also has an inner support of cartilage-like tissue, the endosternite, where certain muscles attach. Most arachnids lack the muscles that would straighten the outer joints of their limbs. Spiders and whip scorpions push their limbs straight with the pressure of their hemolymph. Solifuges and some harvestmen extend their knees using very elastic thickenings in the joint cuticle.

paragraphs.heading: Made for land
paragraphs.text: Almost all living arachnids live on land, although some live in fresh water, and some in the sea everywhere except the pelagic zone. Several traits suit them to life on land. They breathe through internal surfaces such as tracheae, or through book lungs, an internal series of thin vascular plates that swap gases with the air. Other land adaptations include limbs suited to walking on land, internal fertilisation, special sense organs, and a waxy layer on the cuticle that, together with efficient excretory organs, helps save water.

paragraphs.heading: Waste and blood
paragraphs.text: Arachnids get rid of waste through coxal glands along the sides of the prosoma, Malpighian tubules that empty into the gut, or both. Their main nitrogen waste is guanine. What their blood contains depends on how they breathe. Arachnids with an efficient tracheal system do not need their blood to carry oxygen and may have a reduced circulation. In scorpions and some spiders, however, the blood holds haemocyanin, a copper-based pigment that does a job similar to haemoglobin in vertebrates.
